item.title: Why Female Athletes Self-Sabotage and What Helps
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Why Female Athletes Self-Sabotage and What Helps

Self-sabotage may be a learned strategy for navigating sport and gender.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Women and girls in sport receive conflicting messages about what it means to be strong and successful.
  • Self-sabotaging behaviors often function as protection from failure, criticism, or shame.
  • Athletes cannot eliminate every critical thought, but they can choose to do hard things anyway.
  • Self-compassion is not soft; it helps athletes recover from mistakes without abandoning themselves.

A podcast episode explored why women and girls in sport self-sabotage. An equally important question is: Who taught them that they need to?

From a young age, girls receive conflicting messages about how they are supposed to think, look, and behave. Be confident, but not cocky. Be strong, but not too muscular. Be competitive, but still likeable.

But being an athlete inherently challenges many stereotypes about women.

Think of how young girls play. They play with the boys, run fast, get dirty, fall down, get back up, and care far less about how they look. Sports are a space where girls get to be fierce and strong without wondering whether it makes them less desirable. Somewhere around adolescence, we start to see a shift.

It's almost like watching young girls start to shrink themselves, both in sport and in life, to fit everyone else's expectations.

Around this time is also when we start to see young women in sport become increasingly concerned about mistakes, appearance, and whether they are "good enough." Pressures are also felt externally, as perfectionistic pressure from coaches and parents is associated with greater perfectionistic concerns among youth athletes (Fleming et al., 2023).

In the most extreme but exceptionally common scenarios, women take a sideline from sport altogether.

Source: John Arano / Unsplash

Girls disengage from sport earlier and at higher rates than boys, with body image concerns, gender stereotypes, and sport environments among the top reasons (Matheson et al., 2023; Slater & Tiggemann, 2011).

We are Not Going to Banish Self-Sabotage

During the podcast, we also explored whether women can learn to banish self-sabotage.

While that sure sounds nice, it's just another unrealistic standard that we'd be setting female athletes up to fail at.

We have tried getting rid of critical/self-sabotaging thoughts, and it does not work particularly well. In fact, it just promotes more self-criticism, judgment, and shame when those thoughts inevitably show up.

Instead, we can recognize the difference between self-sabotaging thoughts and behaviors.

While we may not be able to stop women and girls in sport from wondering if they'll ever be good enough, we can encourage them to do the hard things anyway, rather than not try at all.

In the end, it would help us all to banish the idea that we always have to act on self-sabotaging thoughts. Instead, we should see them for what they are:

  • Not always true
  • Almost never helpful
  • Almost always informed by external messages about what it truly means to be “good enough”
Source: Jordan Bergendahl / Pexels

When Self-Sabotage Is Self-Protection

Self-sabotage often serves as self-protection.

This explains why some athletes never maximize their full potential, end their careers disappointed, or even quit sport altogether.

If I don't try my best, then my best wasn't what failed. If I don't train as hard as I can, commit myself entirely, recover properly, or fuel myself adequately, I have an explanation if things don't work out.

Most athletes are not doing this consciously. In fact, it's often the opposite.

As I explain in the podcast episode, one of my favorite quotes comes from Theodore Roosevelt: "The credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena."

What I think athletes can take from this quote is one simple fact: You're in the arena.

You've already shown up. You've worked hard, you're uncomfortable, and you're taking a risk. You've already done the hardest thing. In many ways, you've already won.

So why not be as brave as you can possibly be now that you're already there?

Comparison Is a Terrible Scoreboard

I'd be remiss not to talk about how much of a role comparison culture plays in all of this.

It's tricky, because sport drives comparison culture. There is always a ranking, score, record, or opponent. Somebody wins and somebody loses, every single time.

Source: Cristian Camilo Estrada / Pexels

I have to remind people that most athletes lose.

Take it from Roger Federer's famous commencement address. He shares that while he is celebrated as one of the best tennis players of all time, he won exactly 54% of the individual points in his career. He lost 46% of them.

Is Roger a failure? Is he not good enough?

In the end, only one person or one team wins, and most of us lose. If being perfect (aka winning) becomes the requirement for being "good enough", we're all going to be left very disappointed.

Self-Compassion Is Not Soft

Mindfulness and self-compassion in sport are increasing in popularity.

I'll admit that while I spent a lot of time apprehensive about these tools, viewing them as "soft," I've changed my mind.

These tools are active as heck.

Research increasingly suggests that self-compassion can help athletes respond more adaptively to failure, reduce self-criticism, and support psychological well-being without requiring them to abandon achievement (Kuchar et al., 2023; Stamatis et al., 2020).

Self-compassion requires us to remain strong in our worth in the face of failure.

In fact, I'd argue that there is nothing stronger than showing up for yourself with self-compassion and grace after losing a close match.

Just look at how many athletes can't do it.

Maybe the Athlete isn't the Problem

While this conversation focused primarily on women and girls in sport, these topics transcend gender.

Athletes of all genders struggle with perfectionism, comparison, and fear of failure.

It's also no secret that gender occupies a complicated place in sport right now. So not only are concerns about perfectionism and self-sabotage present for all athletes, they are especially heightened for athletes who have complicated relationships with their gender.

It's even more complicated for athletes navigating racism, ableism, xenophobia, economic inequity, and other forms of scrutiny and exclusion.

So instead of asking why athletes keep getting in their own way, we should ask what they learned would happen if they became too powerful, too visible, too muscular, too competitive, too confident, too different, or simply fell short of perfect.

Then we can help them recognize those messages for what they really are and commit to doing the thing anyway.

For more on this conversation, check out How to Defeat Self-Sabotage + Bolster Self-Confidence with Drs. Tess Kilwein & Erin Ayala.

item.title: What Does Childhood Trauma Have to Do With White Supremacy?
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

What Does Childhood Trauma Have to Do With White Supremacy?

High levels of adverse early experiences are found among extremists.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Juvenile offenders and extremists have experienced more childhood trauma than the general population.
  • Right-wing extremists experienced higher rates of childhood adversity than left-wing extremists.
  • Extremists may develop a lack of empathy as a response to maltreatment.

On September 1, 2026, 17-year-old Sarah Santiago, a high school student in North Carolina, was charged with murder in the deaths of three people in a mass shooting at a mosque in San Diego. She and the two gunmen coordinated a plan for her to livestream the event. The two shooters, 17 and 18 years old, one wearing Nazi insignia that Sarah provided, took their own lives. Little is known about Sarah Santiago’s family, her childhood, or those of the gunmen, but researchers have made some headway in understanding the origins of violent extremism.

Young people who engage in any kind of criminal behavior are likely to have experienced many more adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) than those who don’t. For example, 96% of offenders in the Florida juvenile justice system experienced at least one ACE in their lifetime and 40% experienced four or more (Windisch, 2022). Those who engage in right-wing extremism look similar in terms of trauma exposure.

In one of the first studies of the incidence of childhood trauma among white supremacists, researchers found that 65% of those studied had been exposed to at least one type of childhood maltreatment, including physical or emotional neglect, or emotional, physical, or sexual abuse. One third of them were exposed to three or more of these. Notably, emotional neglect and lack of support were reported more frequently and painfully than neglect of physical needs (Windisch).

Another study reported that right-wing extremists experienced higher rates of cumulative childhood adversity than left-wing extremists and greater severity of those experiences. Those who engaged in right-wing extremism were more likely to report aggressive conduct behaviors in adolescence, whereas most left-wing extremists had not been socialized toward violence in childhood and did not engage in aggressive forms of misconduct. Instead, left-wing extremists became socially withdrawn and alienated in reaction to the absence of emotional support and attachment difficulties in childhood (Logan et al, 2024).

Right-wing extremism, which rejects the notion that all people have equal value and often assigns human worth based on race or ethnicity, is organized around the dehumanization of “others” and a social Darwinist “survival of the fittest.” This perspective may be more appealing to individuals with a history of maltreatment who have learned to cope with adversity through aggression and conflict (Logan et al, 2024).

Researchers identified three frequent responses among the traumatized extremists they studied: a sense of betrayal and inability to trust others; self-blame as a coping mechanism that restores a sense of control; anger that turns to violent action as a way to protect oneself from humiliation or feelings of unworthiness (Windisch et al, 2022).

Another mechanism that may help explain violent behavior, including extremist behavior, as a response to trauma is the presence of what are called callous-unemotional traits. What this looks like is a lack of empathy and guilt and a tendency to manipulate others (Mozley et al, 2018). Callous-unemotional traits used to be thought of as biologically based, but we are coming to understand them as reactions to the pain of abuse. Children protect themselves by walling off unmanageable distress and detaching emotionally from others. The retreat from connection and identification with others offers protection to a child’s inner self, but when you don’t see your victims as human beings like yourself, it is much easier to harm them.

I interviewed a former white supremacist for my book, Before Their Crimes: What We’re Misunderstanding about Childhood Trauma, Youth Crime, and the Path to Healing. I’ll call him Shane. He served 16 years in prison for a brutal drug-related murder committed when he was 16 years old. Shane had six ACE exposures, including sexual abuse, emotional neglect, and an addicted parent.

Shane never knew his father. His mother’s heroin addiction left him alone constantly, and his own drug use began at age 8, progressing to hard drugs by age 12. He longed for his mother’s attention, thinking the calls from school and police about his drugged-out behavior and criminal activity would evoke her concern and care. She enrolled him in rehab, but when that failed, she gave up.

He had been groomed, recruited, and indoctrinated into a hate group when he was ten years old, prepared to be receptive to these ideas by his extended family’s belief that people who were not White should be rejected or even destroyed.

“My mom was sober on and off. My involvement with hate groups was the one thing that hurt her. My drug addiction and my crimes upset her, but they didn’t hurt her. I wanted to hurt her the way she had hurt me, so I threw everything I had into it.”

For many white supremacists, the onset of extremist ideas does not begin with a single event but is generated by the cumulative impact of multiple adverse experiences. We can see the racism of these groups; what we may not see is how they also serve as receptacles of wounds and disappointments that have little to do with the stated aims of their activities (Smith, 2025).
